name: Accelerated orthodontics (AcceleDent / Propel)
lead: Accelerated orthodontics refers to adjuncts used with braces or clear aligners that aim to speed tooth movement and shorten treatment. They are commonly grouped as non-surgical methods, such as cyclic vibration devices (AcceleDent is one brand), low-level light therapy and micro-osteoperforations such as the Propel system, and surgical methods such as corticotomy, piezocision and periodontally accelerated osteogenic orthodontics.[1]

Surgical procedures are intended to injure the outer bone layer and trigger a temporary burst of bone remodeling, called the regional acceleratory phenomenon.[1] Systematic reviews have examined these methods and their harms. According to a Grokipedia summary of a 2023 Cochrane review, evidence that non-surgical adjuncts meaningfully shorten overall treatment is of low to very low certainty.[1]

paras: Cyclic vibration devices apply small oscillating forces intended to stimulate bone cell activity, photobiomodulation uses low-level laser or LED light, and micro-osteoperforations make small holes in the bone to cause local inflammation.[1][8] Corticotomy-assisted orthodontics uses cuts through the cortical bone to speed movement and has a documented history in the literature.[4] Injectable platelet-rich fibrin has also been tested for its effect on canine retraction rate.[9]

Orthodontic tooth movement depends on bone resorption on the compressed side and bone formation on the tension side; accelerated approaches aim to amplify these inflammatory and cellular processes.[1]

A systematic review and meta-analysis assessed minimally invasive surgical procedures for accelerating tooth movement and their adverse effects.[2] Systematic reviews have also examined alveolar corticotomies and compared corticotomy-assisted with conventional orthodontic treatment.[3][6] Surgical approaches have been described as accelerating movement 1.5 to 3 times in some studies but as being supported by limited high-quality research.[1]

Surgical adjuncts carry risks including postoperative pain and swelling.[1] A meta-epidemiological study examined how transparently randomized trials of surgically assisted acceleration reported harms.[5]
A study of 116 YouTube videos on accelerated orthodontic treatment evaluated their characteristics, content, popularity and viewer assessments.[7]

Randomized trials of surgical acceleration have been pooled in systematic reviews, and a 2023 Cochrane review on non-surgical adjuncts is summarized in Grokipedia as finding low to very low certainty evidence of clinically significant time savings.[1][2][3][6] Randomized trials specific to vibration brands are not described in the available sources.

timeline.event: Harold Frost describes the regional acceleratory phenomenon, the basis of surgical acceleration.[1]

card.summary: Vibration, light, bone-perforation and surgical add-ons that promise shorter braces time; evidence for non-surgical versions is weak, surgical ones more effective but invasive.
card.note: Surgical versions add procedural risk; non-surgical evidence described as low certainty.

quick.overview:
Accelerated orthodontics covers add-ons to braces or aligners meant to cut treatment time, from daily vibration devices to light therapy, bone micro-perforations and surgery on the jawbone.

Summaries of reviews describe low-certainty evidence for non-surgical methods, while surgical methods may speed movement more but rest on limited high-quality research.
quick.mechanism: The goal is to boost bone remodeling around the tooth roots, either with gentle stimulation or by injuring the bone surface to trigger a temporary burst of remodeling.
quick.risks: Surgical forms involve pain, swelling and procedural complications; reviews have noted that harms are not always reported transparently in trials.
